catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Pronunciation', sec. E 'Stress and Intonation', book pp. 24-27 (pp. 37-40)
catalog_quote: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress ... The location of the heavy stress (whether on the last syllable, the next-to-last, or one of the earlier syllables) is not predictable in Pashto, and the spelling system does not mark stress at all. To ascertain where the heavy stress is in a Pashto word, the non-native speaker must ask a native speaker how to pronounce the word, and then listen for the stressed syllable. The stress in native Pashto words is generally on the last syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant, and on the next-to-last (penultimate) syllable if the last syllable ends in a vowel ... There are probably as many exceptions to the rule given above as there are words which follow it, however, including the word for the language: 'Pashto' ... One of the sources for the exceptions is the number of borrowings in th…
sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Central Pashto: Bečka 1969, A Study in Pashto Stress (Dissertationes Orientales 12, 133 pp.), the sole monograph on the subject and already on the list of works to obtain. No open copy exists: HathiTrust holds it search-only (in copyright, htid mdp.39015014727625), the Czech National Library's Kramerius digitization is 'private' (DNNT, in-library only), Google Books shows no preview (and blocks snippet queries by automated download), archive.org/Open Library/Crossref have nothing; Harvard has print (Widener Library (offsite storage)). Bibliographic records. Second-hand (Trofimov 2023, held by the project): Bečka pp.57-58 count 68.3% of words as final-stressed/final-tending, with suffix-driven regularities (pp.84, 85, 91-93, 95) — consistent with the catalog's lexical coding; acquisition priority high (a library scan or NKP in-library). search-added and read first-hand: Roberts 2000 (MIT thesis, open on DSpace) p.10 states stress 'is determined idiosyncratically for each lexical item' with final syllable 'the most common location' — confirms lexical, does not supersede Tegey & Robson 1996.

Unless indicated otherwise by an acute accent, primary stress falls on the final syllable of a cited form (the most common location). Becka (1969) provides a good description of stress patterns, but the system awaits a fuller treatment
new_statements.citation: Roberts, Taylor (2000). Clitics and agreement. PhD thesis, MIT, Department of Linguistics and Philosophy.
new_statements.reading: Word stress in Pashto is lexically specified (unpredictable per word), with final-syllable stress as the statistically dominant default. This is a first-hand statement by a fieldworking linguist (Kandahar, Laghman, Kabul, Paktia consultants), general rather than dialect-specific. It confirms the catalog's lexical classification and agrees with Trofimov 2023 (free variable-place stress, final-syllable majority) and with Bečka's 68.3% final-stress count as reported second-hand.

audit.action: check whether this is the same language as another entry
audit.recode_to: no reclassification: lexical stands (David 2014 p.15, Shafeev 1964 pp.5-6, Lorimer 1902 p.v, Roberts 2000, Trofimov 2023 all agree, including for the Middle/Waziri dialects). The fix is identity: either (a) merge cent1973 'Pashto' with the catalog's nort2646 'Pashto, central' record, which rests on the identical Tegey & Robson pages and the identical Kabul-dialect description (two records, one entity), keeping nort2646 as the glottocode that matches the source's dialect; or (b) keep cent1973 as Middle/Waziri-Dzadrani Pashto and re-source it to David 2014 sec. 3.1.3 p.15 + Waziri Tables 5.36-5.37 (held) and Lorimer 1902 p.v (downloaded), with Septfonds 1994 on the list of works to obtain.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the scan we hold (page scan of pp.37-38 and scanned of pp.37-40); locator correct; the independent B the compilers had reached the same result. (2) The deciding work is a 1996 CAL reference grammar tied to teaching materials, impressionistic; for Pashto at large it is not the top source (Bečka 1969 stress monograph, Elfenbein 1997, David 2014 exist) but David 2014, which we hold under sout2649, says the same thing ('assigned lexically', minimal pairs), as do Shafeev 1964 (via SPA 1979, downloaded), Roberts 2000 (held under morphstress nort2646: 'determined idiosyncratically for each lexical item.. final syllable the most common location'), Morgenstierne's EIr article (held under wane1241: 'mobile stress') and Trofimov 2023 (downloaded: free stress, final-stress majority). So the lexical coding is safe and WALS/StressTyp2 concur. (3) The real defect is languoid identity: Glo

sources.citation: Lorimer, J. G. 1902. Grammar and Vocabulary of Waziri Pashto. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. (Google scan, archive.org grammarandvocab00lorigoog)
sources.quote: 'There is a variable, and sometimes marked, syllabic emphasis in the Waziri dialect; but no attempt has been made in the vocabulary to indicate the syllables on which this accent falls; partly to avoid complicating the system of notation, and partly because the correct emphasis can most conveniently be acquired in conversation.' Also p.8: vocative allomorphy 'appears to be due to the different incidence of the syllabic accent'. Only Glottolog-listed grammar specific to cent1973 (Waziri); says accent is variable, gives no rule.
sources.locator: Introductory Note p. v (djvu txt lines ~333-339)

sources.quote: Pashto, like many other languages, has its own stress patterns, which differ from those found in English. In Pashto, stress typically falls on the final syllable of a word.

sources.note: marginal: Acoustic study (duration, intensity) of English noun-verb stress produced by six Pashto-speaking EFL learners; the object is English L2 stress, with Pashto stress at most invoked as transfer background.

sources.citation: Trofimov, Artem A. 2023. O pravilakh udareniia v imennykh osnovakh pushtu [On the rules of stress in Pashto nominal stems]. Journal of Language Relationship 21(3-4): 224-241. DOI 10.31826/jlr-2024-213-407 (open PDF at jolr.ru).
sources.quote: p.224: 'Iazyk pushtu kharakterizuetsia raznomestnym svobodnym udareniem' (Pashto is characterized by free, variable-place stress, unusual among modern Iranian languages). Abstract p.241: original mobile-stress paradigms 'underwent morphologization in Pashto. As a result, the vast majority of modern Pashto forms have stress on the final syllable.' Confirms lexical/free stress; refines the record's hedged 'native-word tendency' into a statistical final-stress default with etymologically conditioned barytone classes (áspa etc.).
sources.locator: p.224 first paragraph; English abstract p.241; literature review pp.224-225 (Bečka 1969: 8-14, Morgenstierne 1942, Cheung 2010)

sources.quote: 'Stress in Pashto is forceful ... and it is free; i.e. in polysyllabic words, it can fall on any syllable. In morphology and derivation the stress can be moved from one syllable to another; i.e. it is mobile.... The stress in a Pashto word is often the only meaning-differentiating mark ... The stress can fall on either a long or a short vowel.' Second-hand (database quoting Shafeev), but it is StressTyp2's cited primary and adds an explicit weight-insensitivity remark.

Stress Placement in English Quadri-Syllabic and Five-Syllabic Suffixed Words and Their Roots by Pashto Speakers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa of Pakistan. International Journal of English Linguistics 7(6): 123-137. doi:10.5539/ijel.v7n6p123
sources.note: An L2 study: sixteen Pashto-speaking college students in Swat read 64 English root and suffixed words from cards, and the authors marked primary stress by ear; -ic and -cial/-tial suffixes were stressed correctly most often, -tory and -cy least. The paper says it sought the effect of Pashto L1 stress (p. 125) but never states where Pashto word stress falls, so it adds nothing to the Pashto entry.
